title: Red Tags, Holding Areas, and Sorter's Remorse
subtitle: Not every thing answers on the spot. Give the honest maybes a red tag and a deadline, let time make the call, and handle the second thoughts before they run the pass.
hands_off_to: Chapter 11 (What to Donate, Sell, Store, Recycle, or Throw Away)
audience: Readers partway through a Sort pass who have made the clear keep-and-release calls and are left with the honest maybes they could not decide, plus the second thoughts that circle after letting go. Busy home keepers and parents. Applying the method, not new to it.
core_promise: Give the items you honestly cannot call a red tag, a holding area, and a decide-by date, and let time make the call so no maybe stalls the pass; then quiet the second thoughts, both the fear before and the rare regret after, without willpower and without shame.
emotional_purpose: Relieve the pressure to feel certain on a schedule. Make not knowing a normal, honest state rather than a failure of nerve, and defuse the fear that guards clutter by showing that a tagged thing is not gone and that regret is far rarer than the fear insists.
practical_purpose: Name the two loose ends left by Chapter 9 (the out box, which waits for Chapter 11, and the genuine maybes, which are today's job), show why forcing a maybe breeds remorse, teach the red tag (what it is, the date you tagged it, and a decide-by date), set up a holding area and match the decide-by date to the item, walk a short worked pass over the two entryway maybes, split sorter's remorse into anticipated and real and answer each, and read the friction meter as an honest hold with a dashed forward projection.
primary_cta: Red-tag one honest maybe right now. On a slip of tape write what it is and a decide-by date, stick it on, and set the thing in one spot out of the way. If you reach for it before the date, it stays; if not, the decision already made itself. Read the chapter free in the online book.
secondary_cta: Read the chapter free online, then continue to Chapter 11, where the out box in the corner, finally full and settled, is routed to where each thing should truly go.
keywords: how to decide what to keep when unsure
secondary_device: The holding area (a time-boxed spot where tagged maybes wait out their decide-by dates) and sorter's remorse (the second thoughts, split into anticipated fear before and rare real regret after)

worked_example.space: the two honest maybes left in your hands at the entryway
worked_example.note: After the clear calls in Chapter 9, only a couple of undecidable things remain, which is normal; the great majority of any real sort is easy yeses and easy noes, and the maybes are the small honest remainder.
worked_example.maybe_one: A good umbrella that was a gift: you never grab it, but releasing a gift feels rude, so the use question alone cannot cut the knot. Tag it, decide-by one season, because an umbrella needs weather to prove itself. Reach for it on a rainy morning and it earned its keep; let the season pass untouched and the gift can move on without guilt.
worked_example.maybe_two: A folding rain poncho used exactly once: might be handy on a future trip, might sit until it perishes. Tag it, decide-by a month or the next trip, whichever comes first. Reach for it and it stays; let the date pass untouched and it joins the out box.

definition: Red-tagging is how you decide the things you cannot decide: label an uncertain item with a decide-by date, set it in a holding area out of the daily flow, and let the deadline answer. Reach for it in time and it earned its keep. Let the date pass untouched and the maybe just became a no.
one_idea_to_keep: You do not have to be sure about everything today. Tag the maybes, give them a decide-by date, and let the one thing you cannot argue with, time, make the call for you.
key_motifs: the third chapter of Part 3 (Sort), handling the two loose ends Chapter 9 left
